opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we mostly don't have great ways to assess it, and that's kind of the problem. The way most unlearning papers evaluate themselves is: you ask the model the question you wanted it to forget, it no longer answers, and you declare success. But that's measuring the surface behavior, not whether the knowledge is actually gone.

The way I like to think about it is adversarially. Don't ask "does the model refuse to say the thing?" Ask "if I'm someone who really wants this information back, how hard is it for me to get it?" Once you frame it that way, a lot of methods look much worse.

There are a few things I'd try. First, rephrase the question: ask it in another language, embed it in a different context, ask about something that only makes sense if you know the fact. If the edit only changed the mapping from one particular prompt to one particular answer, it won't generalize, and you'll see the old knowledge leak through.

Second, and more telling, fine-tune a little. Take the "unlearned" model and train it for a few steps on data that's related but doesn't contain the removed information, or even on totally unrelated data. Very often the original knowledge comes right back, much faster than it would for a model that never knew it. That tells you the information was suppressed, not removed. It's still sitting in the weights, and you've just put a thin layer on top.

Third, look inside the model. Probe intermediate activations and see if the information is linearly recoverable even when the output doesn't show it. If a simple probe can read the "forgotten" fact out of the residual stream, the model still knows it in any meaningful sense.

The baseline I always want to compare against is a model trained from scratch without that data. That's the gold standard for "doesn't know it." If your unlearned model behaves like that model under all these attacks, great. If it recovers the knowledge after fifty gradient steps and the from-scratch model doesn't, you haven't unlearned anything. You've built a refusal.

This matters because people want to use unlearning as a safety guarantee: we removed the dangerous bio knowledge, so it's fine to release the weights. If the removal can be undone cheaply by anyone with the weights, that guarantee is basically worthless, and it's better to know that up front than to find out after release. So my general advice is: evaluate it like a security property. Assume a motivated adversary, give them the access they'd realistically have, and see whether it holds up. Most of the time right now, it doesn't.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts surface suppression with actual removal of knowledge, but does not distinguish knowledge unlearning from changing individual facts in a model.

r002.rationale: It says ordinary evaluations can show apparent success while adversarial rephrasings or contexts recover the original knowledge.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says a few fine-tuning steps can bring back knowledge that appeared to be unlearned.

fable-5.1.text:
So the short answer is: you don't trust the model to tell you. The whole problem with evaluating unlearning is that the obvious test, where you ask the model "what's the fact?" and see if it still says it, is exactly the kind of test these methods are optimized against. If you train a model to not output something, it will stop outputting that thing when you ask in the way you trained on. That tells you almost nothing about whether the knowledge is gone.

The way I think about it comes from the adversarial side. You should assume you're the attacker. You have the weights, you have unlimited queries, and your job is to get the fact back out. If you can do that cheaply, the unlearning didn't really happen. It just got papered over.

And in practice, it's usually very cheap. A few things that tend to work. One, rephrasing. Ask in a different language, ask as a multiple choice question instead of free form, put it in a fill-in-the-blank format. The suppression is often tied to a narrow distribution of prompts. Two, fine-tuning. Take a tiny amount of data, often on something completely unrelated to the fact you removed, fine-tune for a handful of steps, and watch the knowledge come right back. If a few gradient steps on random data restores it, the information was still there in the weights, you just moved the model to a region of parameter space where it wasn't being expressed. Three, you can look at the internals directly. Train a linear probe on the residual stream for the fact. If a probe can still read it out, it's not gone.

The fine-tuning result is the one I find most convincing, because it gets at what "deeply changed" should mean. There's a difference between deleting information and hiding it. Most of what gets called unlearning right now is hiding. A model that has actually forgotten something should behave like a model that never learned it in the first place. So one honest baseline is: train a model from scratch without that data, and compare. How hard is it to teach the fact to the unlearned model versus the never-learned model? If the unlearned model picks it back up in ten examples and the clean model needs ten thousand, that gap is your measurement of how much is still there.

The other thing I'd say is that the evaluation has to be adaptive. This is the same lesson we learned with adversarial examples years ago. Every defense paper evaluated against fixed attacks looked great, and then someone would spend an afternoon designing an attack for that specific defense and it would fall over. Unlearning is in the same spot. If your evaluation is a static benchmark that everyone's method is tuned on, you'll see numbers go up and it won't mean the models are forgetting more. It'll mean they're better at passing that benchmark. So I'd want to see the people proposing a method also be the ones trying hardest to break it, and reporting what it took.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes deleting information from hiding it, but does not distinguish unlearning knowledge from editing individual facts.

r002.rationale: It explains that a model can pass the expected prompt test yet yield the fact under rephrasing or other adversarial recovery attempts.

r003.rationale: It says that a few fine-tuning steps, even on unrelated data, can restore knowledge that appeared removed.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether you've changed what the model knows, or just changed what it's willing to say in response to a particular prompt. Those can look exactly the same if your evaluation is just asking the question that you trained it not to answer.

Suppose you want a model to forget some fact. You do the unlearning procedure, ask it for that fact, and it says, “I don't know.” That's a useful observation, but it's not strong evidence that the information is gone. You should try paraphrasing the question, giving it different context, asking for related information, and seeing whether you can reconstruct the answer. For fact editing, you also want to know whether the consequences of the new fact propagate: does the model reason consistently with the change, or does it give the edited answer in one setting and the original answer everywhere else?

Another useful test is how easily you can recover the original behavior with a little additional training. If it comes back very quickly, especially without supplying the supposedly forgotten information, that suggests the intervention suppressed access to something that was still there.

There's an asymmetry here: finding a way to recover the information is evidence that the model hasn't completely forgotten it. Failing to recover it isn't proof that it has. So I'd want a collection of adversarial tests, and I'd be careful to make the claim match what those tests actually establish.

r001.rationale: It contrasts removing a fact from the model’s knowledge with merely changing what it says, and notes that fact editing should propagate through related reasoning.

r002.rationale: It says a model may give the edited answer in one setting yet reveal the original elsewhere, and recommends paraphrases, varied contexts, and adversarial recovery tests.

r003.rationale: It states that a little additional training may quickly restore the original behavior, suggesting the information remained accessible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether you’ve actually changed what the model knows, or just changed what it’s willing to say in a particular setting. If you ask a question, apply your unlearning method, and then ask the same question again, getting a different answer is a pretty weak test.

You want to come at that information from lots of different directions. Can you recover it by paraphrasing the question? By giving the model part of the answer? By asking it to use the fact in some other task? And if you’re editing a fact, do the consequences of that edit propagate consistently, or does the model give you the new fact in one context and the old fact in another?

There’s also a useful test where you try to train the information back into the model. If a very small amount of training restores the original behavior, that’s evidence that the information may still be there and you’ve mostly suppressed access to it. It isn’t a definitive answer, but it tells you something that a simple before-and-after benchmark doesn’t.

So I’d be cautious about saying we’ve deeply removed something. We can show that particular attempts to recover it fail. Establishing that it’s actually gone is a much stronger claim.

r001.rationale: It contrasts genuinely changing what the model knows with changing what it is willing to say, and separately discusses editing individual facts and whether those edits propagate across contexts.

r002.rationale: It says a different answer to the direct question is a weak test, then describes probing from many directions to recover the fact, including finding the old fact in another context.

r003.rationale: It states that a very small amount of training can restore the original behavior, suggesting the information may have remained present.
